headline: Commission discussed wetland buffer fill request at 5 Roby Street, scheduled a site walk, and approved August 4 minutes as amended.
summary: The commission heard a presentation from Eric Newman about filling and stabilizing 1,435 SF of wetland buffer at 5 Roby Street to manage knotweed, with a site walk set for September 14. Members also discussed invasive species control at Terrell Farm, Buckmeadow, Joyce Park, and Greeley Park, and reviewed an ongoing tree-cutting infraction at 102 Flint Lock Drive.
decisions: Approved the August 4, 2026 minutes as amended.

NASHUA CONSERVATION COMMISSION 
September 2, 2026 
 
A.  Call to order

to order on Wednesday, September 2, 2026 at 7:00 PM, 229 Main 
Street, City Hall. 
 
B.  Roll call  
 
Members present:  Sherry Dutzy, Chair 
                         Dick Widhu, Vice Chair 
Carol Sarno

D.  Old Business:

E. New Business: 
 
Eric Newman, 5 Roby Street. Proposal to fill, grade and 
stabilize 1,435 SF of the wetland buffer for a prime wetland, to 
create a small level back yard, while controlling invasive 
knotweed. Map 126. Lot 23. Zone R-A – Urban Residence. Ward 6.

Eric Newman, the owner of 5 Roby Street led a presentation on his 
request to fill, grade, and stabilize 1,435 square feet of wetland 
buffer for a prime a prime wetland to create a small level backyard 
while controlling the invasive knotweeds. Mr. Newman purchased 
the property in June of 2025 and encountered a massive infestation 
of Japanese knotweed, which he described as a six-foot sea of 
Japanese knotweed next to his driveway. In September of 2025 Mr. 
Newman began manually digging out the root systems without 
chemical herbicides due to safety concerns for his dog, son, and 
the nearby wetland ecosystem. Rob Sousa, City of Nashua Code 
Enforcement officer, was alerted and informed Mr. Newman to cease 
all work within the regulated zone and required. Mr. Newman 
consulted with Deb Chisholm who provided him with information on 
the restrictions, setbacks, and recommended hiring a wetland 
expert. Mr. Newman stated he is not looking to build on this area 
and more to possibly provide a safe children’s play space and to 
store a small boat and canoe. 
 
Mark West, a certified wetland scientist from West Environmental 
in Nottingham, NH introduced himself and presented that he was 
hired to formally delineate the wetland boundaries on the 
property. Mark West stated that no trees have been cut during the 
work. The site maintains a mature forest canopy for the first 35 
feet along the wetland boundary. Mr. West emphasized the 
importance of leaving the canopy of trees, which actually provides 
shade and may help a little with the reduction, and expansion of 
knotweed. The burning bush in the shrub layer will be left. The 
topography features an abrupt downslope leading to a steep, 15to 
20-foot drop-off from the flat work area down toward the wetland. 
The upper portion of the wetland contains historical fill and 
functions as an active groundwater seep. Two large storm drains 
at the end of Oakland Ave discharge high volumes of stormwater 
into the wetland, creating an active system, depositing sediment, 
and causing scouring. 
 
Mr. Newman expressed he was not provided any notice of the site 
being a former federal asbestos waste disposal site upon purchase 
of the home in June of 2025. Nor was there anything on the title 
or deed. Deb Chisholm provided information that this site was 
capped with a protective barrier that is partially located on the 
property, extending onto neighboring properties at 15 and 17 East 
Dunstable and to the south. This capped asbestos area does not 
extend into the current planning or work zone and will not be 
disturbed.    
 
Mark West indicated that the outer portion of the buffer zone was 
disturbed during the initial manual removal of the knotweed.

Protective and restorative measures include planting native shrubs 
and maintaining the mature pine and oak trees to preserve the 
wetland shading, stability, habitat, and runoff protection. The 
property features a larger natural buffer to the wetland compared 
to adjacent houses further down the street 
 
Commissioner Sarno asked if all of the knotweed was within the 
buffer. 
 
Mr. Newman responded saying that a lot of it is in the buffer. He 
was able to manually remove about 75% of the knotweed behind and 
next to the garage (outside the buffer zone) during his first year 
of ownership. Mr. Newman noted that chemical applications have 
been avoided and stated he is strongly against the use of chemicals 
for this control because of the nature of the sensitive area.  
 
DISCUSSION ENSUED ABOUT PHOTOS PROVIDED AND THE LOCATION OF THE 
KNOTWEED WITHIN THE BUFFER AREA AND WHAT IS STILL THERE. 
 
Commissioner Sarno asked what procedure was done when dealing with 
this knotweed. 
 
Mr. Newman explained he researched control methods through global 
knotweed support group of scientists and homeowners. Methods 
evaluated included chemical sprays, stem injections, plastic tarp 
smothering (deemed unfeasible due to the steep slope), and digging 
and burying.   
 
DISCUSSION ENSUED ABOUT THE DISPOSAL OF THE CLEARED-OUT KNOTWEED 
 
Commissioner Dutzy asked what Mr. Newman intended on doing with 
the level space. 
 
Mr. Newman responded by stating he did not have any intention of 
planting grass or lawn there. Bring in soil to continue to manage 
it. Possibly wood chips to place a small playground in the future.  
 
DISCUSSION ENSUED ABOUT THE FILL BROUGHT IN AND A TREE NEAR THE 
FILL AREA. 
 
Commissioner Darby asked what kind of fill was brought in, what 
percentage was filled and what percentage more is left to fill 
in. 
 
Mr. Newman stated he had 40 yards of clean, rocky soil, with no 
debris or trash fill brought in from James Longa of Merrimack, 
NH.  And about 40 additional yards of clean fill are required to

complete the leveling work and extend the knotweed management 
area.  
 
DISCUSSION ENSUED ABOUT TARPING THE KNOTWEED IN THE ASBESTOS AREA. 
 
Site walk is scheduled for Monday, September 14th, at 5:30pm 
 
F. NCC Correspondence and Communications 
 
 
G. Commissioners Discussion 
JOYCE PARK TRAIL CLEANUP: 
 
Commissioner Widhu spoke about leading an invasive plant clearing 
at Joyce Park along with a couple of volunteers. The target date 
is the end of September. Commissioner Dutzy encouraged other 
members to volunteer to scout out the areas needing attention and 
to help with the cleanup. Commissioner Darby volunteered.    
 
 
STUDENT DAYS OF SERVICE PLANNING: 
 
Commissioner Sarno led a discussion on two major volunteer events 
scheduled for local student groups. 
• Rivier University Day of Service: Saturday, October 3, from 
9:45am-12:45pm. 
• Bishop Guertin (BG) Day of Service: Thursday, November 5th, 
from 9:30am-1:30pm. 
 
TERRELL MEADOW MAINTENANCE AND EQUIPMENT STATUS: 
 
Commissioner Dutzy attempted to mow at Terrell but the lawnmower 
would not start. She will inspect the mower over the weekend to 
determine if the engine was flooded. If it remains non-
operational, they will transport it to Mike Maynard’s shop for 
repair. Heavy vegetation growth has occurred along the walking 
trail leading up to the restored meadow. The commission previously 
hired a professional brush hogger in 2018. The historical 
recommendation is to brush hog the meadow every three to five 
years to halt woody plant succession. 
  
BUCKMEADOW MAINTENANCE PLANNING: 
 
Commissioner Sarno lead a discussion about Buckmeadow due for 
periodic maintenance. The landscaper who cleared the boardwalk at
NCC 
September 2, 2026

Buckmeadow is working on an estimate to complete the brush hogging 
work. He will need to rent the necessary heavy machinery. 
 
INVASIVE SPECIES MANAGEMENT AND STRATEGIC PLANNING:  
 
Commissioner Sarno lead a discussion recommending the hiring of a 
professional to draft a comprehensive, long-term invasive species 
management plan.  
 
DISCUSSION ENSUED ABOUT DEALING WITH ALL THE INVASIVE(S) 
 
 
The commission reviewed external planning resources:  
• The Belmont Conservation Commission hired an outside 
professional to conduct a comprehensive invasive species 
assessment. 
• The Town of Merrimack partnered with the Nashua Regional 
Planning Commission (NRPC)to develop an invasive species 
management plan.  
• The Merrimack Trails Committee is currently developing a 
similar plan.  
 
Terrell Farm and Buckmeadow Road are the priority target areas. 
Joyce Park is heavily infested but is considered “beyond help at 
this point.”  
 
Two members will research professional contacts from Merrimack 
and Belmont, request a site walkthrough, and secure quotes. 
Municipal rules require three competitive quotes for expenditures 
of $5,000 threshold. 
 
102 Flint Lock Drive Infraction: 
 
Commissioner Dutzy asked Deb Chisholm for an update on the 
unauthorized tree cutting that was done on this property in 
September of 2025. The matter remains on hold due to a similar 
ongoing infraction case. 
 
DISCUSSION ENSUED ABOUT REVISING THE LAND USE CODE TO ADDRESS 
UNAUTHORIZED CUTTING.  
  
GREELEY PARK MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION:  
 
Commissioner Darby discussed that he is on the Greeley park 
advisory board. There is a dense pine forest behind the park that 
contains significant deadfall and storm debris. Some community

members oppose any tree cutting, while others argue the forest is 
unhealthy. Commissioner Darby was looking for clarification on 
Conservation Commissions role on this advisory board. The 
conservation commission recommends that the Park Commission 
undertake a formal forest management plan. 
  
DISCUSSION ENSUED ON THE CONSERVATION COMMISSIONS FOREST 
MANAGEMENT PLAN.
